utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-R77.4, the Prosecutor versus Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber still owes you a decision on D1 and D2, two statements, the one initially tendered under 92 bis and the other one under 92 ter. The Chamber does not admit D1 and D2; leaves it, however, open that the statement given by Mr. Schook for which a 92 bis admission was given under the condition that the attestations would be there, that if the Defence would provide the attestation within seven days, the Chamber will, even though the presentation of evidence is closed, will admit that document and will consider that document as well, but not the other one which was originally tendered under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful to Your Honours for that indulgence. I don't envisage that we will be availing ourselves of that opportunity. We have made quite some efforts to get the address of Mr. Schook, and we haven't been able to do so. I may call on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. The Chamber will wait a week and see whether matters change or not. Then, today, I think what we will hear is the closing arguments by the Defence and then there will be an opportunity for brief responses and perhaps further questions by the Chamber. Mr. Dieckmann, are you the first -- yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. Just in relation to the brief responses, do you envisage after the Defence closing speeches the Prosecution have a right to reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would be the case, of course, you would have an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Last word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to have a last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although, that is not in common law not a well-known principle; and, of course, if there's no need to add anything. And, Mr. Saxon, of course, it also depends on whether something new comes up. I mean, there's no need to repeat anything, of course, of what you've already said before. Mr. Dieckmann, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, as the Defence has been allocated 30 minutes in which to make its closing arguments, I will try to be as concise as possible. I shall begin with some evidentiary matters. In light of the oral arguments yesterday of the Chamber in support of rejecting our joint Defence application for leave to appeal the decision on the admissibility of Morina's interview, in which the Chamber clearly stated that at this stage of the proceedings, a decision from the Appeals Chamber decision does not materially advance the proceedings, and I refer to page 99, line 25, and page 100, line 2, the Defence is not seeking leave to appeal the decision regarding Bajrush's motion to exclude the intercepts of the discussions between the protected witness and Morina; however, we would like to state for the record that the Defence reserve our right to raise it before the Appeals Chamber post judgement. We also wish to inform the Trial Chambers that we intend to submit a joint request for reconsideration of the decision on Morina and Haraqija second request for a declaration of inadmissibility and exclusion of evidence, and we are in the filing procedure. The Defence of Bajrush Morina holds the view that in light of the circumstances of this case, which have been finally highlighted in this trial, the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Bajrush Morina's conduct was likely to dissuade the protected witness from giving evidence, nor that it was of similar gravity as the other forms of contempt set out in Rule 77(A)(iv). Regarding additional legal arguments with respect to the framework of Rule 77, the Defence refers, to save time, to its Defence pre-trial brief, para 34 up to 37. Your Honours, first and foremost, it has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt that Bajrush Morina interfered with Witness 2 in any manner regarding his testimony in the case of Ramush Haradinaj. As Witness 2 confirmed in his testimony this week, he agreed to give the mutual friend of Bajrush Morina and himself his telephone number, which Bajrush Morina had requested. We refer to page 127, line 2. The witness gave out this piece of information freely, being aware that Bajrush Morina is a political journalist from Kosova from the newspaper Bota Sot. We refer to page 113, line 18 and 19. When Bajrush Morina called the Witness 2 on his telephone number and asked for an urgent meeting the next day, the witness did not hang up. We refer to page 129, line 2. I may quote the witness: "No. My intention was not to hang up. We did talk and I explained that it was impossible to meet the following day." In the contrary, the witness offered another date to meet in the very near future, the 10th of July. We refer to Exhibit P7, para 3. In fact, Witness 2 wanted to meet with Bajrush Morina. We refer to Exhibit P8, para 15. Witness 1's testimony on trial gives evidence that Witness 2 told him that he would not testify in the Haradinaj case if this meeting was not allowed, referring to page 81, line 23. Witness 1 described Witness 2 as curious after having received the phone calls from Bajrush Morina. We refer to page 82, line 10. Another circumstance that has to be taken into account when evaluating whether an incident can be regarded as an interference due to the criterions of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is the fact that the meeting between Witness 2 and Bajrush Morina took place in full agreement between the Prosecution of the ICTY, the police of the third country, and the Witness 2. This consensus was confirmed by Witness 1, I may quote: "Q. So we can summarize in the end, there was a consensus of the Prosecution of the ICTY, your superiors, and the witness that this meeting could take place? "A. Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. And on the contrary, if the Prosecutor had disagreed, the police of the third country would not have accepted the meeting. We refer to page 82, line 4. With regard to the meetings on 10th and 11th July, 2007, Witness 2 confirmed that Bajrush Morina did not scare him at all. I may quote: "I didn't feel intimidated or under pressure because the meeting with Bajrush was a friendly meeting. We met as old friends." I refer to page 140, line 21 up to 23. During the course of his evidence on 9th September 2008, Witness 2 confirmed that he was disappointed with the way of contempt investigations against Bajrush Morina, how it were conducted by the ICTY. We refer to page 140, line 1 up to 3. Witness 2 confirmed that he had told the police of the third country that he had been in contact with Bajrush Morina after his interview on the 26th of October, 2007. Page 135, line 2 and 3. Witness 2 was very much concerned about Bajrush Morina's situation who has expressed fears regarding his security and mentioned health problems he got from the interview of the 26th of October, 2007. We refer to page 138, line 10 and 11. Witness 2 was upset about the situation of Bajrush Morina and informed the police of the third country that he perhaps would not be in contact with the ICTY anymore under these circumstances. Page 138, line 12 up to 15. Thus, the Prosecutor was not able to satisfy the threshold of Rule 77(A)(iv). Regarding the aforementioned and confirmed attitude of Witness 2, the expressed consensus of the ICTY and the police of the third country, the alleged conduct of Mr. Bajrush Morina was not of a similar gravity as the other forms of contempt set out in Rule 77. Your Honours, the Prosecution has not proven that Bajrush Morina acted knowingly and wilfully. I would like to refer to the Brdjanin Judgement where the Trial Chamber held that the mens rea for otherwise interfering with the witness requires proof of the accused's knowledge that his conduct is likely to deter a witness or a potential witness from giving evidence or that his conduct is likely to influence the nature of the evidence. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber held that Rule 77(A)(iv) requires that the conduct was carried out with a specific intent to interfere with witnesses. The Prosecution seemingly tries to infer the accused's intention to interfere with the protected witness from the alleged delivery of the messages that the witness was one of the, I may quote "only three people" who can save Ramush Haradinaj and that the witness should withdrew his testimony. However, the Prosecution has not proven beyond reasonable doubt that the accused actually knew whether Witness 2 was going to testify in the Haradinaj case. The Prosecution also infers the accused's specific intent to interfere with the protected witness from his alleged question put to the witness about his travel to The Hague. The Prosecution did not prove that Bajrush Morina asked the question to the Witness 2, I may quote: "When are you going to The Hague?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I apologise. The relevant statements in evidence are not consistent in this matter. Witness 2 mentioned this question in the statement dated 20 September 2007, Exhibit P8, para 7; as well as in an interview with the police from the third country from 3rd July 2007 which Witness 2 confirmed in his testimony on 9 September 2008. This is page 133, line 5. However, when Witness 2 was interviewed by an ICTY Prosecutor on 17 August 2007, he did not mention this question allegedly put to him by Bajrush Morina at all. This statement from August 2007 is Exhibit P7. This is striking because in the light of his statement from 20th September 2007, this question would have been the reason for him to contact the police of the third country. Very briefly, therefore, for the Defence, it has not been established beyond reasonable doubt that Bajrush Morina had any prior knowledge about a testimony of Witness 2 in The Hague in this specific procedure. In addition, the accused did not have any motive to commit an offence under Rule 77 by interfering with Witness 2, who at the time was about to give evidence in the Haradinaj case. Several witnesses gave evidence that Bajrush Morina has neither been a member of the party of Ramush Haradinaj, nor that he has ever been a supporter of the party of Ramush Haradinaj. We refer to the witness statements of Angjelina Krasniqi, page 162, line 4; and the statement -- and the testimony of Mr. Kasapolli, page 312, line 5. On the contrary, Bajrush Morina has always been a supporter of the former President Rugova. We refer to the testimony of Angjelina Krasniqi, page 162, line 1; and Mr. Kasapolli, page 312, line 2. So Bajrush Morina had no personal interest in committing a crime in order to save Ramush Haradinaj. The final argument against the assumption that Bajrush Morina had the intention of committing contempt by meeting Witness 2 is that Bajrush Morina had a strong individual motive of his own to meet Witness 2. According to his testimony from 9 September 2008, Bajrush Morina informed Witness 2 that he intended to meet with him in order to speak about the interview he had conducted with him in 2002. This is page 133, line 12. Witness 2, as well as Angjelina Krasniqi and Mr. Kasapolli, described Mr. Morina as a professional journalist and former editor-in-chief of Bota Sot. We refer to the testimony of Angjelina Krasniqi, page 161, line 20; Witness 2, page 113, line 18 and 19; and Mr. Kasapolli, page 311, line 24, as well as page 312, line 8 to 10. As a professional journalist, Bajrush Morina wanted to find out whether Witness 2 still stood by his interview. The reason for this was that Bajrush Morina was unable to get an official final authorisation of the final version of this interview from Witness 2 in 2002, because the witness had to leave before it could be obtained in 2002. We refer to page 120, line 5 to 6. According to the revised transcript of the conversation of Witness 2 and Bajrush Morina from 10 July 2007 - this is page 4, line 13 up to 15, and page 17, line 34 of the English version - Witness 2 and Bajrush Morina immediately talked about this interview. And on page 17, Witness 2 explicitly confirmed that he stood by it. This intention of Bajrush Morina to initiate this meeting was mentioned by Bajrush Morina during the interview of the 26 October 2007, before he was confronted with the audio-tapes recorded in the third country. I refer to page 7 of the revised transcript of the interview with Bajrush Morina from the 26th October 2007. Nevertheless, the question of the interview was never considered in the investigations undertaken by Witness Mitford-Burgess. In fact, this witness did not even make the effort to obtain the interview during the investigations. We refer to page 188, line 9. Hence, he did not investigate any other possibility in this case except that it was a contempt of court from start to finish. We refer to page 213, line 3. In fact, Witness Mitford-Burgess confirms that the investigations did not explore alternative motives or alternative explanations for the activities and behaviour of Bajrush Morina in July 2007. We refer to page 213, line 3. In this circumstances, it is notable that Bajrush Morina, in fact, published an article in Bota Sot about his trip to a third country. The publication of this article was confirmed by Witness Mitford-Burgess. We refer to page 212, line 7. The publication of this article shows that Bajrush Morina travelled to the third country for professional reasons. The fact that he travelled to the third country was public and he did not hide it in his home country. This evidence in relation to the interview from 2002 raises serious reasonable doubts as to the alleged intention of Bajrush Morina under Rule 77. So it cannot be excluded that he, in fact, decided to instigate a meeting with Witness 2 in order to find out whether Witness 2 still stood by this interview from 2002 and to write another article about the third country or make research for further articles. As far as the Prosecution rely upon the audio-tapes and transcripts of the 10th and 11th of July, 2007, which have been produced by the police of the third country, the Defence submits that the weight of this material must be evaluated with greatest caution. It has been shown that this material was, in fact, produced illegally, views the opinion of the Defence. Witness 1 confirmed that the audio-recordings of the conversations between Witness 2 and Bajrush Morina on the 10th and 11th of July, 2007, constituted a violation of Mr. Morina's right to privacy. We refer to the answer of Witness 1 on page 83, line 7. On the other hand, this witness confirmed that there is no legal provision adopted by the parliament of the third country allowing audio and video-recordings of private conversations in this time, of summer July 2007. We refer to page 88, line 4. Under Article 8 II of the European Convention of Human Rights, a violation of privacy is only allowed if it has been prescribed by law, and we don't think that this criteria has been met in this case. Regarding further legal arguments on this matter, to save time, we refer to the Confidential Astrit Haraqija's and Bajrush Morina's joint application for leave to reply and joint reply to Prosecution's response to Bajrush Morina's second request for a declaration of inadmissibility and exclusion of evidence with confidential annexes a through J from 1st of September, 2008, para 5 and 6. Witness 1 referred in his testimony to "travaux preparatoire" of the third country. We refer to page 85, line 15. This "travaux preparatoire" does not substitute a law in the sense of Article 8 II, European Convention of Human Rights. Therefore, in the opinion of the Defence of Bajrush Morina, this material was produced in violation of Article 8 II and is illegal. Secondly, the transcript of the interview with Bajrush Morina from 26 October 2007 is also of limited weight. The first reason is that Bajrush Morina did not explicitly and sufficiently waive his right of counsel. The second reason for this being that Witness Mitford-Burgess confronted Bajrush Morina during this suspect interview with an excerpt of the audio-tapes of the conversation recorded by the police of the third country in July 2007. We refer to page 184, line 10. Witness Mitford-Burgess testified that he did not so without knowing the legal basis of the origin of this material, but he testified that he trusted the assertion of the police of the third country that this material had been produced legally under the law of this country. We refer to page 18 6, line 23 to 25. After the confrontation with this material, Witness Mitford-Burgess did not inform Bajrush Morina again about his rights to be assisted by legal counsel. The Prosecutor refers in his closing arguments to parts of this transcript from 26th of October, 2007, but part of the transcript after the confrontation of Bajrush Morina with this material from the third country. The Defence holds the opinion that it cannot be excluded that Bajrush Morina, being confronted with material that is inconsistent to his interview before, went back to an account that was consistent to what was recorded just to avoid further pressure by the investigator in this unpleasant situation. This attitude is not a rare occurrence in criminal procedures. Your Honours, the burden that must be discharged by the Prosecution to support the finding of contempt is proof beyond all reasonable doubt. This standard and burden of proof has not been met by the Prosecutor; and, therefore, it is our submission that Bajrush Morina must be acquitted. Anyhow, the following mitigating factors have to be taken into account with regarding sentencing: The good character of Mr. Bajrush Morina, which has been confirmed by Witness 2, Angjelina Krasniqi, and the Witness Kasapolli; the fact that he is a father of four children and has to take care for his two sick and old parents; the lack of a criminal record; and his cooperation during the time of provisional. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann, for your closing arguments. I see that you did not even use your full time. Mr. Khan, are you ready to deliver your closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you give me a moment, please. If it please Your Honours, on the 29th of April of this year, you will recall conducting, Mr. President, the initial appearance. Mr. Senior Prosecuting trial attorney Re attended on behalf of the Prosecutor; and at page 13, line 18, he said that: "The Prosecutor is trial-ready. No further investigative work to do." He continued at page 16: "The only further material we have to give is the witness testimony of the protected witness, and we will give this," to the Defence he meant, "this afternoon." Twenty-nine disclosure batches later the OTP, in my respectful submission, is no further forward in assembling anything approaching a coherent, never mind a compelling, case. But what is the Prosecution's case? In summary, it is simple. It is that on an event in Peja, that's paragraph 12 of the pre-trial brief, at a cultural event in Peja, my client told the second accused to go to a third country and tell the protected witness that is subject to the proceedings in this case not to give evidence. What is the evidence the Prosecution put before Your Honours in order to convict my client? It is Bajrush Morina. And that, Your Honour, is the start and end of the Prosecution's problems in this case when it comes to assembling a case against my client. The Prosecution concede at page 5, paragraph 18 of their pre-trial brief, that it was Morina that applied in writing to go to the third country. There has not been a scintilla of evidence presented by my learned friend to show that that trip was approved by my client, except the evidence that comes from the mouth of Bajrush Morina or is repeated by others based upon what Bajrush Morina is said to have said. The Prosecution called Angjelina Krasniqi. She accepts that the document she approved was based upon Bajrush Morina's say so. She accepts that there is no independent confirmation that my client ever uttered a word about the proposed trip or contacting the proposed witness, except based upon her acceptance of what Bajrush Morina said. Your Honours, the OTP rely upon SMSes and telephone intercepts between her and the second accused. They suffer from the same malady: They come from Bajrush Morina. Your Honours are well familiar with the law; but, with your leave, I will address you very briefly on controlling cases on the treatment of hearsay evidence that is relevant, in my submission, in this case. In Lucca, Italy, in 2001, 36 European Human Rights Reports, 807, at paragraph 40, the European Court said, and I quote: "Where a conviction is based solely or to a decisive degree based on depositions that have been made by a person whom the accused has had no opportunity to examine or have examined, whether during the investigative -- investigation or at trial, the rights of the defence are restricted to an extent that it is incompatible with the guarantees provided by Article 6." Your Honour, that case law has been fully embraced by the law of this Tribunal. Your Honour, in the Trial Chamber in Prlic, in its decision on the request for admission of statements of Jadranko Prlic, 22nd of August, 2007, stated: "The Chamber stresses the importance of the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, as adopted by the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal, whereby a Chamber may not base a conviction solely or substantially upon evidence not subjected to cross-examination. The Chamber recalls the decision on the admission of evidence does not cast any judgement upon its probative value. It will take into account of the possible lack of cross-examination when determining the probative value to be accorded to the statement and will demand corroborative elements before giving it any weight." Your Honour, there's case law from the Popovic case. I will cite one, well, from the Popovic case. I will move on just to one final matter so as not to waste time. The Appeals Chamber in Prlic, in its decision on the appeals against the decision admitting the transcript of Jadranko Prlic -- Jadranko Prlic's testimony, I do apologise, in its decision on the appeal against the decision admitting the transcript of Jadranko Prlic's questioning into evidence, 23rd of November, 2007, at paragraph 4, held, and I quote: "Unacceptable infringements of the right of the Defence in this sense occur where a conviction is based solely or in a decisive manner on the depositions of a witness whom the accused has had no opportunity to examine or have examined, either during the investigation or at trial. The European Court of Human Rights applied this reasoning to the statement of a co-accused in pre-trial proceedings in a case where neither the applicant nor his lawyer had been given the opportunity to question the co-accused at any stage of the proceedings." Your Honour, the Prosecution's burden is a heavy one. It's well-known that the standard is beyond reasonable doubt, but it is the respectful submission of the Defence that Your Honours give life to the standard and apply it in a very real sense in this case. The Prosecution, of course, had problems in Haradinaj. It was accepted by the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, you will know that this was an agreed fact by the Defence as well, but the Prosecution cannot simply bring a case and state in effect that because we had problems in Haradinaj and there is some suggestions that it was -- there were difficulties, we can convict anybody we drag and haul before this Court. They are seeking to castigate and besmirch the good reputation, the good character of my client. They have made him defend allegations he knows nothing about. Perhaps, Your Honour, he can be -- perhaps Your Honours can understand why he feels aggrieved and why his evidence is that he has felt under such stress. That was his evidence in the box yesterday, and we are putting a translation request in that on the opening day, he did say that I feel -- the transcript reads: "I feel offended to be here." We're going to seek clarification. The word as I understand it is that: "I feel embarrassed or mortified to be here." Your Honour, one could understand if one was in the position of the accused how he feels so harshly done by. Your Honour, I don't for a moment say that the Prosecution have concocted evidence. I don't say for a moment that they have somehow told Witness 2 what to say. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: My principal argument, as Barack Obama may put it, is they simply don't get it. They don't get that when you bring a case of this magnitude before an international court, you must properly investigate it. Your Honours must feel that you have no option except to convict. On this case, you are free to acquit for numerous reasons. Your Honours, the Prosecution do not discharge this burden by asking you to uncritically accept hearsay evidence. They don't discharge their burden by asking you to accept a travel document. It was at tab 11 from Angjelina Krasniqi which has Mr. Haraqija's name on it, and not asking a single question as to how she got that document or why that document was not in the official archives of the ministry, despite the fact that the police officer said, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, that he was given full cooperation by the ministry, no suggestion by any tampering or anything hidden by the ministry by the Prosecution witness. The Prosecution don't prove their case by asking Your Honours to turn a blind eye to the fact that not one document presented after extensive and expensive investigation does not have my client's signature on it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly requested to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will, and I'm not reading. Just one moment. It's the French, I know. Your Honour, the Prosecution do not prove their case either by asking Your Honours to turn a deaf ear to the fact that no independent corroborative witness has been presented that can say they either heard my client instruct the second accused to go to the third country or that he heard my client mention the name of Witness 2 or that my client wished himself to go to the third country or that my client in any way, shape, or form wished to tamper with any witness before the Court. Your Honours, as far as the telephone intercepts between the second accused and Angjelina Krasniqi and the interview with the Prosecution, the Defence will simply state the blindingly obvious, that multiple hearsay from the same source does not get any better by this simple repetition, neither any better nor any stronger nor any more believable. Your Honour, you have, of course, heard from Mr. Mitford-Burgess, and I am not going to go over points in too much detail. But, Your Honours, it seems unfortunate that the Prosecution in effect would have you -- would have -- well, the Prosecution in effect adopt a Guantanamo-esque position, if I can put it like that. They say that the law of the third country doesn't apply because the contempt was not before any court in that third country, and they say, well, the law of the Tribunal doesn't apply because no request has been obtained under Rule 77 from a Trial Chamber. So what is governing the communications between the OTP and the authorities of the third country and the investigative practices? This is rather unfortunate and is a matter perhaps that Your Honours would wish to speak to when giving final judgement in this case. Your Honour, given the terminal problems, in my submission, that the Prosecution have got, what did they do to fill in the holes? Well, they didn't seek any surveillance of my client in July, in August, in September; they didn't check his computer; they didn't check his fax; they didn't speak to the permanent secretary; they didn't even get the article that was written in 2002 by the second accused. The office hadn't even read that article, beggar's belief in my submission, beggar's belief, that an article that was raised in interview hasn't even been read by the officer investigating the case. But what he does say is that from the surveillance they had, no incriminating evidence has been obtained against my client, nothing from his phone, nothing from the archives that were searched from the ministry despite the full cooperation that was given, nothing from Steven Schook. And, of course, perhaps one can pause there for a moment. The Prosecution accept that their evidence against Schook was similarly based on hearsay. They looked at his computers, they looked at his telephone, they conducted -- contacted the office of internal affairs; and they concluded, quite properly, that his good name stands, his name is not besmirched, and he is not worthy of prosecution. What is source - it's an American expression of course, so forgive me for that - what is source for the goose is source for the gander. What helps the American, Mr. Schook, and saves him from being unnecessarily made to defend proceedings? It should be source for the gander when it comes to Mr. Haraqija and Your Honours' discretion and, in my submission, my strong urging, to acquit him of all counts. Your Honour, particularly when the Deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations is in, of course, a quite dominating position and a position of influence, the Prosecution's position of course is simply -- well, in part because my client was a head of a ministry of which the second accused worked as the political advisor to one of his subordinates, therefore somehow they can cobble together a case that implicates my client. It's ludicrous and untenable, and, legally, it doesn't pass muster, in my submission. What other investigative options were pursued by the Prosecution? The Prosecution's officer in the case has admitted - he admitted, Your Honours, under oath - that they did not purview any other investigative options. Your Honours, I'm going to ask you to consider this in the context of Haradinaj, the problems they were having in trial, concerns that maybe their case had not been adequately proved, allegations of witness intimidation and uncertainty, a Prosecutor going to the Security Council, and constantly criticising UNMIK, constantly blaming others for the difficulties she had to properly investigate and prove a case that she brought. But, Your Honours, the Prosecution never asked the second accused if he could have had a misunderstanding, if he could have spoken to the first accused and misunderstood completely. It was never put to Bajrush Morina by the Prosecution that Angjelina Krasniqi had said that he had sought permission from my client. Instead, the Prosecution rather bizarrely did it the other way around. They conduct two interviews with my client, and yet they put it to Angjelina Krasniqi that the interview with the first accused -- with the second accused is correct. It's a completely wrong way of doing it. Instead of trying to make the evidence better at source, they do it in a completely back-handed and inappropriate way, in my submission. Your Honour, no suggestion, no investigation regarding the corruption angle in this case. Shocking. OTP investigators sit silently on their hands, content that you will simply on a wish and a prayer convict people they bring before you when. They do not properly investigate the evidence of their own witnesses. Your Honours, I refer you to page 5 of the 7th of November, 2007, interview with Angjelina Krasniqi. And, Your Honours, just bear with me for a moment. I may read from it, in fact. Your Honour, she says: "This was a personal visit of Bajrush; however, because of the financial situation, he asked me to cover expenses. This is an abuse of office, but we did make an application for these expenses to be covered, although it wasn't an official journey."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And a redaction is to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that a redaction be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Page 18, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: "This wasn't an official journey because official journeys can't be made to countries unless those countries issue invitations." Now, Your Honour, this must be viewed together with OTP Exhibit 18. And, again, they're silent on this because it causes them problems, but they don't even investigate it; and that, of course, is where there's a conversation between Angjelina Krasniqi and the second accused, and there's discussion of creating invitations. Now, Your Honours, I'm not here to prosecute the case and I'm not here to make any allegations against the second accused, but I am here to point out significant and real investigative possibilities that were simply not pursued by the Prosecution in breach of their overriding obligation to properly and diligently bring cases before this Court. Your Honours, of course, there's no duty, like in the ICC, to investigate exculpatory evidence, but there is a duty to properly and diligently prosecute. Your Honours, good investigative practice shouldn't have been sacrificed on the altar of the Haradinaj trial or pre-conceived notions of guilt. Your Honour, there's no inquiry into the journalism of the second accused and whether or not that played a part. The Prosecution say very openly that the second accused was the political advisor to Prosecution witness Krasniqi; yet, they also say he was a journalist. And just step back for a moment, Your Honours. Why is it that the full focus of the Prosecution investigation is in relation to my client and not any investigation has been conducted in relation to the other cap the second accused wears, which is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, I stop you for a second. You made a reference to page 18, line 20. That is not clear to me, and since there's urgency in the matter, I would like you to verify the exact line and page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are referring to an earlier page, I signed an order for a redaction in relation to this. I do understand that you've received --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- an e-mail on the matter. I just wanted to make sure that we have not overseen anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours are ever vigilant, and I'm grateful to you and also Mr. Monkhouse for his great assistance, as ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Not at all. Your Honour, as I was saying, there was no attempt by the Prosecution to investigate the investigative aspects of this case, and I won't repeat what I said regarding the 2002 article. And you will refer, no doubt, in your deliberations to my hopefully very brief cross-examination, where I put it to the witness that the account suddenly and dramatically changed when the witness was confronted with the surveillance in the third country, but that no investigation at all took place in relation to the article that the second accused had written in 2002, that he had mentioned as being one of the motivating factors of going to the third country. Your Honours, of course, I do say one of the motivating factors, he did know the protected witness and he did say in his interview, if one relies upon it at all, that he was trying to kill two birds with one stone. But, Your Honours, I am -- it's flabbergasting, in fact, that the Prosecution didn't even get that statement -- that interview, but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. What is the second bird that he wanted to kill?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, he said he also knew the second accused and they're friends, so it was to visit a friend as well. That was my reading of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, perhaps no more flabbergasted than an investigation in which the officer in the case prepares transcripts that are used to convict a client, at least at first instance, before clarification, but transcripts that are prepared by somebody who doesn't even know the language. All these matters, I think, should be considered in the round regarding have the Prosecution seriously and diligently investigated this case in the manner that they could? No questioning at all, no inquiry as to whether or not there could have been a motive of the second accused to name-drop by mentioning Schook, mentioning Haraqija, in order to show that the groups he moves with. Your Honours, I'm not again making any allegation against the second accused and I'm not are prosecuting this case. I am simply saying that there is doubt. These are areas, these are doors which a diligent Prosecutor should have closed. They have not closed. The evidence was missing and it remains missing. Your Honour, it's viewed in stark reality, perhaps, or in very stark contrast by just looking at what happened in the third country. Thirty officers are detailed, they suspect that a crime may be committed, there's a danger. The Prosecution have it that the second accused rang my client. They knew the hotel. Is there any intercept from the hotel? Has a phone record been given from the hotel showing that the second accused rang my client? They searched the premises in UNMIK. Have records been given of a phone call between the second accused and my client from his mobile phone? Not a scrap of evidence. Your Honours cannot turn a blind eye to such blatant and fundamental and fatal omissions. They would have you believe that my client was planning to go to the third country. Where's the flight reservation? Where is it? Any evidence from any staff member of the ministry? No. Any documentary evidence from the ministry? No. Any evidence from an airline that a reservation had been made? No. Case built completely and utterly and improperly on conjecture and speculation and a pre-conceived notion of guilt. Your Honours, the Prosecution state yesterday - and I didn't follow it, I must admit - but they mentioned in their closing and in the cross that Bajrush Morina stated in his interview that: "I didn't really lie all that much. I said I spoke to the minister and, in fact, I spoke to the spokesman." Well, you haven't heard from the spokesman. But how much of a lie, I wonder, does the Prosecution need before they say there's doubt? On what basis once they admit there's a lie do they ask you to accept in good faith that a transcript, not under oath, by a suspect can be believed to incriminate and convict an innocent man? Your Honour, this case, of course, is not so serious compared to Articles -- the offences that Your Honours may try under Articles 2 to 5 of the Statute, not serious in the sense of gravity, number of victims, scale; but the consequences to my client are profound. He's a young man. I would ask you to bear in mind the character evidence that you had before you. He's a man that in some respects, I would say, is part of the future of Kosova. And a conviction by this Court has very critical consequences to his political career in Kosova, to even issues like travelling and getting on a blacklist of the United States. Your Honour, the Prosecution can't ruin somebody's life and besmirch an individual's character on such flimsy evidence. Your Honour, in summation, to convict my client, you must reject the sworn evidence of the accused. You must ignore the evidence of OTP Witness Krasniqi, who states that she never spoke to my client regarding the third country or the second witness, and that she never heard my client discuss that trip or that person with any other individual. Your Honours, you must close your eyes to all these problems and focus on the untested and untried evidence of the second accused. Your Honours, I pause very briefly. There's one red herring that was thrown into this case. It's the fund. You will see the UNMIK interview, which is being put by the Defence, it's Defence Exhibit 4. That's an interview conducted well before this crime is alleged to have been committed. My client was interviewed not as a suspect, as a witness. Your Honours, will see the account he gave is completely and utterly candid and completely and utterly consistent with the account he has given in the box. Your Honour may well understand that there were political problems regarding the LDK and the Haradinaj coalition. The fact that the LDK is viewed by and is bitterly hated by some segments in Kosova and is viewed as not being supportive of the war. And, in my submission, the reasons given by my client for associating himself with that fund are compelling and natural, particularly when the Prosecution have not controverted the clients's very close link, personal link, as well as party link, with Ibrahim Rugova. So that's a complete red herring, in my respectful submission. No charge has been brought before him by UNMIK to know about the matter. It's, again, an attempt by the Prosecution to cobble together disparate pieces of evidence to put forward it rather a Frankenstein of a case, and it would have you convict it. Your Honour, it's not important and it should not be accepted. Your Honour, the paradox of this case is the Prosecution-style witness is so compelling a man that they wish to throw him in prison for a year. The Prosecution don't seem to get the irony of that; I do hope Your Honours do. Your Honours, I don't intend to address you much on sentencing. It's my submission, my very strong submission, that Your Honours have no option, in good faith, but to acquit on this flimsy evidence. But my client was an individual, a KLA fighter, who turned to the LDK; a Kosovan Albanian who put an arm out to the Serb community; building bridges - it may sound like a cliche - but building bridges by helping to rebuild some of the damage of 2004 and the churches. The Prosecution would have you see my client only through the prism of their allegations in a bid to prove this case. Your Honours, I would ask that you give this case the most anxious scrutiny individually before you decide if you should convict my client. In my respectful submission, there is absolutely no basis in law or in fact to deprive my client of his liberty a moment longer. Your Honour, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we first, if there are any questions, to put them to the parties so they can include in their final observations their answers to those questions. Judge Moloto has one or more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question to Mr. Dieckmann, but Mr. Khan you can also answer it because you also referred to it. Could I just be reminded, do we have any evidence that the article of 2002 was ever published; and if so, when was it published the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I explained on the first day of this trial, the Defence itself received this article on the Wednesday before the trial started, and we initiated a translation of this article. And as far as I'm informed, this article was published in 27th of August up to -- sorry, in the end of July up to the beginning of August in five parts. And we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It was immediately published after the interview was made, and there was a final version and this was published then, yes. And we have shown this article, with leave of the Chamber, to the witness and ask him to confirm that this is the article that was published then, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a specific question for you, Mr. Khan. Rather central in your argument is that you should not use the statement of a co-accused for several reasons. I'm referring to footnote 27 of your pre-trial brief. You say this is equally true for the common-law tradition and the civil-law tradition, and you refer to Dutch case law and Italian Code of Criminal Procedure. Now, you might not be surprised that I looked into this Dutch case law. Isn't it true that the practice in Dutch court has been for 80 years that by an administrative act - some call it a trick - well, at least by an administrative act that the whole concept of co-accused doesn't exist anymore in the Netherlands and that co-accused nowadays are accused who are tried simultaneously with other accused, and that the rule saying that you couldn't use the evidence of one accused against another accused, he can use it only against himself, that that actually is a dead letter. And even in one of the cases you are quoting - and I'm referring to the 1953 case - that in the official annotation published together with the decision, that the annotator, who by the way was the judge in the Tokyo Tribunal earlier during his career, says, Why not change the law if already for so many years we do not apply it; and, therefore, that is well-established case law for 80 years now which invalidates the legal provision, and that your cases you are quoting are rather confirming that this is the situation rather than a practiced exclusion of statements of co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be reckless and impertinent and completely inappropriate for a Pakistani and British-qualified lawyer to second-guess a former Supreme Court Judge of the Netherlands. So to the extent the pre-trial brief is wrong regarding Dutch law, I don't rely on it. But, of course, I fully accept in totality Your Honour's interpretation of Dutch law. I can't speak to it. As far as to English law, of course, I can speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The rule has been clear that the evidence of a co-accused is not evidence against another co-accused unless he takes the stand. If the second accused takes the stand and can be cross-examined, of course, it can be evidence. We haven't had that opportunity, and that is why we say, in compliance with Lucca in Italy, and the jurisprudence I cited, Your Honours cannot convict on it because you would have to in order to convict rely a completely or in a very significant part upon that evidence that we have not been able to get behind and challenge. But, Your Honour, regarding Dutch law, I'm grateful for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Returning to the civil-law tradition, and let's not focus on Dutch law, isn't it true that usually accused who do not take the stand are not giving any evidence under oath --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... that the situation. Therefore, since you say it's not only the common-law tradition but also in the civil-law tradition that this rule applies, that the very basis, as you just explained to us how it works in the English tradition, that that is totally foreign to the structure of civil law-oriented procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps not, because whilst the common law and civil law or Franco -- Romano-Germanic system may try to achieve justice by different routes, at fundamentals they have raised similar protections. The case that was cited, Lucca in Italy, of course, apply to a civil-law country. And what the European Court of Human Rights made crystal clear, as confirmed by this Appeals Chamber, is the right to confrontation need not be in the courtroom; but if it's not in the courtroom, we must have had a right to confront at the investigative stage. We have not had such a right here. This is of course a sui generis court, it's a molded hybrid system, but we haven't had that right, and an accused in many civil-law systems, of course, must answer questions. So, Your Honours, the right to confront is the core issue, and this is a right to which we have been denied. And it is for that reason, in compliance with Strasbourg case law, the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal, and in common sense, in my respectful submission, that Your Honours cannot rely on that evidence by itself in order to convict my client because you simply cannot be satisfied so that you are sure, particularly given the way that this case has been investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Italian criminal procedure since 1991 is more common-law oriented than civil-law oriented, more adversarial than inquisitorial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but, of course, European court is not -- its judgements are not applicable to common-law systems or civil-law systems. They are applying the Convention, which is applicable to a broad spectrum of countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I was just, since you were referring to Italian --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course. Your Honour is quite right, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you were referring to Italian criminal procedure as well. I just wanted to have this context clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have no -- yes, I have one question for you, Mr. Dieckmann, which is the following: You told us that the recording in the third country of the conversation was illegal; and then on page 12, line 12, you continue to say that -- and you were then talking about the interview, so that immediately following your submissions on the recording in the third country you said, "The record of the interview is also of little weight." This confused me a bit because apparently on the recording in the third country, you said it was illegal; and, of course, we've heard all the arguments about that. Then for the second you say it's also of little weight. Now, what, finally, is your position? Could we use it? We have given decisions at the time there was no reason to exclude, which, of course, is a first decision before trial. Now, what's your position? Can't we use them or should we give little weight to them, because you confused me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm sorry for this confusion. Exactly. First of all, in the first step, we tried to reach exclusion of the recordings of the interview from the 26th of October, 2007. But, nevertheless, the things we tried to present as a foundation for this motion has to be taken into account by evaluating the weight of these recordings. And due to our opinion, it is not a reason to exclude this recordings for the judgement or for eventually conviction. Due to my understanding of the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, it's not automatically that illegal produced material that is used in another interview would lead to a complete exclusion of this material. But the fact that our client, due to our understanding, has posed several questions at the beginning of this interview from 26th of October, 2007, to the investigator before he clearly understood what is -- what are the arguments against him, and the fact that this material was used on page 17, you can see it on the recording, that the material was used against him and material was shown to him without another information if he wants to continue without legal representative, if he wants to continue with this interview. These factors of this recording, of this interview, have to be taken into account if you evaluate what is the result against our client from this interview. It has to do with the weight and not with the exclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now the recording of the 10th and 11th of July, you say they were illegal, you've explained that to us. Should we give limited weight to them as well, or on the basis of what we heard at trial you take a different decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: We read carefully the decision of the Chamber and we think if there is no exclusion, of course, the circumstances of the production of this material must be taken into account. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann. Usually, if I addressed the registrar, you can imagine it's not without reason. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think I was finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the case, you can't misspeak anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one advantage, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have put questions mainly to the Defence, Mr. Saxon. I'd like to give you two or three minutes, perhaps not to repeat everything, but if anything knew came up. If you say I need five or six, that's fine; then I would give a similar possibility to the Defence. And I urge all the parties not to repeat anything, but just to add what is relevant and with what came up during these closing arguments as well as new. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours. And I may need that five or six minutes. First of all, Your Honours, my learned friend Mr. Khan argues that there was no independent evidence to -- the only evidence upon which you can convict Mr. Haraqija comes from the mouth of Mr. Morina, and that there is no evidence to show that Mr. Morina's trip was approved by Mr. Haraqija except for the words of Mr. Morina. That's not quite correct, Your Honour, and I would respectfully ask you to give some attention to what is now P9, the interview of Ms. Krasniqi with the Office of the Prosecution on the 7th of November, 2007. My learned friend relied on it a few moments ago. In the English portion page 7, lines 1 to page 8, line 12; page 9, line 2 to page 10, line 15 in the Albanian, where Ms. Krasniqi told the Office of the Prosecutor that the minister approves all official journeys, either orally or in writing. And Ms. Krasniqi confirmed that this declaration was correct before this Trial Chamber two days ago. My learned friend says that there is no documentary evidence submitted by the Prosecution from the Ministry of Culture implicating his client, Mr. Haraqija. Again, I would respectfully ask the Chamber to direct its attention to Exhibit P22, the very first page, the request for travel authorisation, in the name of Mr. Morina and Mr. Haraqija, with the words written by Ms. Krasniqi that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That didn't come from -- the evidence of my learned friend's own police officer was that didn't come from the archives, that came from Ms. Krasniqi. I said no evidence from the ministry. That came from Krasniqi. The officer didn't know where she got it from. That was very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have an opportunity to further respond. Mr. Saxon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With respect to the comment of my colleague Mr. Dieckmann that in the first meeting between Witness 2 and Mr. Morina, that they were discussing the 2002 interview, and he referred you to page 4 and page 17 of the recording of that first meeting on 10th of July. Well, the lines referred to on page 4, lines 13 to 15, that part of the discussion actually refers to recent articles which Witness 2 had sent to the editor of Bota Sot. They're not speaking about the 2002 interview. Again, if you look at page 17, line 34, where it's true Witness 2 says: "I stand by the prior interview," that discussion is occurring in the context, Your Honours, of whether Witness 2 will withdraw his evidence against Mr. Haradinaj. Please see the text of the same page lines 1 through 22. Your Honours, my learned friend has criticised the members of the Office of the Prosecutor for not first going to the Trial Chamber last year to get an order of the Chamber to investigate. Well, Your Honours, these meetings in July were recorded by the police according to Witness 1 for two reasons: To ensure that the witness would be available to testify before this Tribunal and to protect his safety and security. This was in no way investigation by proxy by the OTP. Second of all, Your Honours, it's impossible for the Prosecution to come to a Trial Chamber with a blank slate and say, Please give us authority to conduct a full contempt authorisation. There must be some information in hand at the time, and that is the information that the Prosecution presented to the Trial Chamber in August of last year. With respect to the comment of Witness 1 that the recordings of these meetings were a violation of Mr. Morina's right to privacy, it's clear, Your Honour, that Witness 1 is not a legal expert. He was speaking as a police officer. And so it's unclear whether such a legal opinion, if that's what it was, should receive much weight from this Trial Chamber. By the way, finally, my colleague Mr. Khan referred to the intercepted telephone conversations, recorded telephone conversations, between Ms. Krasniqi and Mr. Morina, describing them as multiple hearsay. Well, Your Honours, that evidence may be hearsay; however, Ms. Krasniqi confirmed the accuracy of those recordings and the subject of the discussion in those recordings in her statement to the OTP. And she confirmed those declarations before the Trial Chamber two days ago, Your Honour. Therefore, Your Honours, in our respectful submission, the Trial Chamber may and should find both accused guilty as charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you. First of all, again to the question of the weight of the evidence, I would like to clarify that, of course, as a question of the evaluation of the weight; but, on the other hand, the Defence of Bajrush Morina cannot imagine that a decision of the Chamber could be based on material and evidence that was produced on the violation of Article 8 II of the European Convention. This is our point. Of course, it has to be evaluated, the weight; but we think the weight would be at such a minimum that an adequate decision for our client could not be based on it. The second point I would like to address is the point my learned colleague Mr. Khan made regarding the quality of investigations regarding our client. If you look in the closing argument of the Prosecutor from yesterday, and I refer to page 327 and 328, 327, line 25; and 328, first line, then you can see that the Prosecution definitely did not have a view of the position of our client. They investigated only in one direction and everything that has to do with the interview, with the -- being a professional journalist was not in the focus of the Prosecution. The Prosecution has not an understanding of the complexity of this situation; and therefore, we think because of this lack of investigation, the evidence that has been produced in this trial could not be used against our client. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be brief. A close scrutiny of the interviews, in my submission, simply doesn't support the Prosecution's contention. Your Honour will see that on numerous occasions, Ms. Krasniqi states that, for example, at page 2, page 8, page 13 of the 7th of November interview, that she'd been told by Bajrush Morina that he'd been given permission. She says at page 3 and page 4 that she's responsible for signing. And she says repeatedly that she didn't have confirmation from any other source that permission had been given or authorisation obtained. She also said in evidence that authorisations are made valid by the permanent secretary, not by Mr. Haraqija. Your Honour, there's no evidence to support that my client knew that Mr. Morina was travelling to the third country. Your Honour, regarding the second matter by the Prosecution, I don't accept for a moment, with the greatest of respect, my learned friend's contention that the reason they couldn't go and get an order of the Trial Chamber to investigate was because it was too wide or carte blanche, or whatever word he used, because he states at that time -- and the investigator said, Witness 1 said, that this is a witness that was subject to protective orders, this is the Prosecution's case, that nobody knew the witness was going to be coming to The Hague, and yet a phone call had been received by somebody who didn't know where he was to the fact that she should come -- and made it clear that that -- that the second accused knew, the Prosecution say, that Witness 2 was coming to The Hague and he wished to have a meeting with a minister. Well, on what basis would a Trial Chamber with this information -- at least an application could have been made for monitoring and for investigation regarding a possible contempt. The Prosecution didn't even lodge the application. They could have been forgiven if they could produce evidence that an application had been given and had been rejected. They didn't even try and comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: (redacted) Trial Chamber. I knew this was not -- there's no property in a witness. It's not the Prosecution's entitlements simply to protect a witness; it's the Trial Chamber's. It's not an arrogation of authority. The Trial Chamber gives these orders to protect these witnesses and the Trial Chamber are trusted and are entitled and obligated to enforce those orders, and he didn't seek such an order from the Trial Chamber because his only contact was the Prosecution. The Prosecution in short didn't do that which they should have done. Regarding the recording, I'll be brief. My learned friend, as I understand it, says that she verified multiple hearsay. Well, it's not true. If one reads what she says, and you can read it when you're deliberating, she says repeatedly that, you know, I know it all by hearsay. This is page 10 -- sorry, she says repeatedly that she had sympathy for Mr. Morina, but she doesn't verify what he says; she can't, because she never heard it directly or from any other source outside of Mr. Morina. That's my point. It all comes back to Mr. Morina, and that is insufficient, given the problems I've detailed, for Your Honours to convict in this case. So those are my points. I can go into more detail, but I'm sure Your Honours have got the point, unless you think it's needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, just for me to understand your last argument fully, you would say if someone calls and tries to organize a meeting, that this simple reference: When are you going to The Hague, is that for you sufficient to say possible contempt, which would mean that on the basis of that information without any further conversation that would already be contempt?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not saying that. Of course, I'm not the Prosecutor. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I return this to Mr. Registrar, he has another job already lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Under the law of the third state, that was sufficient to require judicial authorisation to commence the requested surveillance. So, at least under a comparative law argument, as presented by the Prosecution knowing this was an issue, it would be enough. It's for them to decide whether or not they should have sought that order in this case, given the problems, the notorious, they say, notorious problems in Haradinaj and the evidence that they presented in order to give their consent to this meeting, which of course was a sine qua non to the alleged offence that's before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Since we have no further questions, this concludes the trial proceedings in this case, and the Chamber will consider the case and will deliver its judgement in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. It brings us to the issue provisional release pending judgement. Your Honour, I don't know how long Your Honours - and of course it may be unfair at the moment - but I don't know how long Your Honours are intending to take on this. But if it's going to be more than a few days, I would ask perhaps that we can make a -- even an oral application for provisional release. I don't know if my learned friend is opposing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the conduct of the two accused, we will not oppose a request for provisional release at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, an oral application is on the record. May I take it that it's on the same basis as the earlier request for provisional release. Mr. Dieckmann, you would join in that application?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I join the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon. MR. SAXON. I sincerely apologise. But upon further reflection, I must confess the Prosecution has asked that the Chamber sentence these two accused to long terms of imprisonment, very serious sentence. And given that context, Your Honour, the Prosecution cannot simply agree to a request for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan or Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are about turns and very swift about turns, and this was a very swift about turn. The moment of contentment that no doubt my client felt was very quickly reversed, but, of course, the gift is within Your Honours' hands. The Prosecution have asked for two years. We have outlined the huge deficiencies that we say afflict the Prosecution's case. They knew that they were facing allegations -- they knew they were facing allegations of the -- that carried a maximum of seven years' imprisonment at the time they returned to The Hague in fulfilment of the provisional release that Your Honours had granted. The Prosecution's case has not grown any stronger in the last few days, in my submission, quite the reverse. There is no reasonable prospect, in my respectful submission, that the -- my client would either fail to surrender to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal for judgement or that he would interfere with any other victim witness or other person. That hasn't transpired since the indictment and since the period of provisional release. No grants have been put forward by my friend. Most critically, of course, just the nature of the sentence by itself is not a compelling argument. This, of course, is not a pre-trial sentence. If Your Honours find that the accused are guilty, no doubt you will convict them, and they will serve whatever sentence you deem appropriate. But at that moment, the assumption of innocence stands, and there are no coherent arguments, in my submission, that would militate against a grant of provisional release in circumstances where UNMIK have stated - and you have it on record - that they have satisfactorily complied with all conditions. There's not been a whisper from the Prosecution that any victim witness or other person had been harassed or intimidated, and there's been nothing other than full cooperation with the authorities to comply with all orders of the Trial Chamber. In those circumstances, I do submit that a compelling case has been put forward if Your Honours are so minded to grant provisional release until Your Honours have liberated this matter reached a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I completely support and join the submissions of my learned friend Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have concluded the trial already. I announced already that we would deliver our judgement in due course. We have now in addition to that on the record an application for provisional, which is contested by the Prosecution and which was further argued by the Defence. We'll also give a decision on this application in due course. We stand adjourned sine die.
